turns.text: Hello Daniel, come in. Have a seat. Where would you like to start today?
I don't really know. My GP suggested I come. She said I look exhausted, and she's right, I am.
What does exhausted look like for you?
Like I'm running on fumes. I work as a project manager at a logistics company, and I've been completely burned out since October.
Since October. Did something happen then?
Not one thing. We lost a big client, and half the team got moved onto the rescue plan, so I ended up doing three people's jobs. I just never came back up after that.
What does a normal working day look like now?
I'm at my desk by seven and I'm still answering messages at ten at night. Even when I'm not working I'm thinking about work.
That's a very long day. How is your sleep?
Terrible. Most nights I sleep about four hours. I wake up at three in the morning and can't fall back asleep.
What happens when you wake at three?
My head just starts. Shipping schedules, the client, whether I've forgotten something. Then I look at the clock and do the maths on how little sleep I'm going to get, which makes it worse.
And then?
Then I lie there until about five and get up and make tea. I've started dreading the nights, if I'm honest.
That sounds draining. Is there anything else going on in your life besides work?
Yes. My father. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in the autumn.
That's a lot to carry alongside everything else. How is he?
He's still himself, mostly. His hands shake, and he's slower, and he gets frustrated. He's seventy-three and he's always been the strong one.
And how are you involved in his care?
I'm the one who drives him to the hospital in Leeds. The neurology appointments are every few weeks, and it's an hour each way.
Is there anybody who shares that with you?
Not really. My younger sister Hannah lives in Toronto, so all the care for our father falls on me.
How do you feel about that?
Guilty for even saying it. She calls him every Sunday, and she's not the one who's neglecting him. It's just that I'm the one who's here.
Can you say more about the guilt?
I feel it's selfish to be tired when he's the one who's ill. So I don't say anything to anyone.
Not to Hannah either?
She asks how I am and I say fine. What would be the point? She can't do anything from Canada.
What would you want her to know, if you said it?
That I'm not fine. That some days I sit in the car park at the hospital for ten minutes before I go in, because I can't face it.
That's an important thing to notice. What happens in those ten minutes?
Nothing, really. I just breathe. I look at the other people going in. Everybody looks tired there.
You mentioned your GP. What did she say?
She did blood tests, and they were all normal. She said it's stress and exhaustion, and asked if I'd thought about talking to someone. I said I hadn't got time.
And yet you're here.
My girlfriend booked it, to be honest. Claire. She said she was done watching me disappear.
How is it with Claire?
She's very patient. She makes me tea and doesn't push me to talk. But I can see it's wearing on her too.
In what way?
She stopped asking if I want to go away for the weekend, because I always say no. That's the thing I feel worst about, actually.
What stops you saying yes?
The emails. If I'm away I'll come back to two hundred of them. And Dad might need something.
So even rest has a price.
Yes, exactly. I can't remember the last time I was properly off.
What did you do for yourself before October?
I ran. Ten kilometres every Saturday morning. I'd done it for six years.
And now?
I stopped about two months ago. My legs felt like lead, and then I just never went back.
How do you feel about that?
Like I've lost a part of myself. It was the one time in the week nobody could reach me.
What would it mean to get some of that back?
A lot, probably. I just can't picture where the time would come from.
Let's leave that for a moment. What is your relationship with your boss like?
Peterson. He's all right as a person, but he sends emails at eleven at night and expects an answer before breakfast.
What do you do when one arrives?
I answer it. Every time. Even if I'm in bed. Claire hates it.
What are you afraid would happen if you didn't answer?
That he'd think I wasn't committed. There's a restructuring in the spring and I'm afraid they'll let me go.
And if they did?
I don't know. I think part of me would be relieved, and then I'd feel horrible about being relieved. I have a mortgage.
Both things can be true.
I suppose so. I've never said that out loud.
How are your moods apart from the tiredness?
Flat, mostly. And irritable. I snapped at a colleague last week over nothing and went and sat in the toilets for ten minutes.
What was happening for you in those minutes?
My heart was going and my hands were shaking. I thought for a second it was a heart attack, but it passed.
Has that happened before?
A couple of times. Once on the train to Manchester. I just had to get off and stand on the platform.
That sounds frightening.
It was. I haven't told anyone about it, not even Claire.
Thank you for telling me. What are you afraid it means?
That I'm losing it. That I'm going to end up like, I don't know. Not coping.
Have you noticed anything that makes it worse?
Coffee, probably. I'm on about six cups a day. And I've started having wine in the evenings to switch my head off. Two glasses, sometimes three.
How do you feel about the wine?
Uneasy. It works for an hour and then I wake at three anyway. I know it's not helping.
You are noticing that clearly. That is useful.
It doesn't feel useful. It feels like I'm just listing everything that's wrong with me.
I hear a person who has been holding a great deal on his own for a long time. What was it like to say it today?
Strange. A bit of a relief, actually. Like putting down a bag I didn't realise I was carrying.
What do you carry that you'd like to put down first?
The nights, I think. If I could sleep I could probably cope with the rest.
We can start there. Did anything about your family growing up shape how you handle this?
My grandfather worked in the mines in Yorkshire. He never complained about anything, not once. Dad's the same. You just get on with it.
And you?
I'm the same. I keep thinking he would think I was weak for being here.
What would you say to him if he were here?
That I'm not weak. I'm just very tired.
That sounds like something you could say to yourself as well.
Maybe. I don't know if I believe it yet.
That's fine. You don't have to. Let's think about what we could do between now and next week. Would you be willing to try something small?
Depends how small. I haven't got much left.
Very small. A fixed time in the evening when you switch off your phone, even for twenty minutes.
Peterson would hate that.
What would actually happen in twenty minutes?
Nothing, probably. He wouldn't even notice.
Would you try it?
Yes. Half past nine, perhaps. I could make it a thing with Claire. Tea on the sofa.
That sounds good. And a note of how the night goes?
I can do that. I'll write down when I wake up, if I wake up.
We're nearly out of time. How are you feeling now?
Tired, but lighter. Is it normal to feel a bit shaky after saying all that?
Very normal. It takes energy to say it out loud.
Right. Thank you. I think I needed to hear that.
Same time next week?
Yes. I'll be here. I'll try to make it on time, the trains are awful.
